source_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
exact_quote: SDAG (Dekel et al., 2026) replaces standard causal attention with sparse document attention, so that one malicious document is less able to influence other retrieved evidence.
A_rationale: The claim describes SDAG's mechanism: replacing standard causal attention with sparse document attention to limit cross-document malicious influence. This matches both the Section 4.3 text and the Figure 4 categorization of SDAG under attention/interaction control. It is a faithful descriptive statement of the cited method's design contrasted with the causal-attention baseline. No numeric or directional overreach is present.
A_evidence: Section 4.3 Post-Retrieval Isolation, PDF p.9; Figure 4 taxonomy p.8 (SDAG under Attention & Interaction Control, O1)
B_rationale: Section 4.3 identifies the architectural substitution, and Figure 4 classifies SDAG as an L3 attention-and-interaction control against integrity attacks. The survey provides no SDAG result table, influence metric, or controlled standard-attention ablation demonstrating that the substitution makes a malicious document less influential. Thus the architectural description is supported, but the asserted causal effect is not directly established.
B_evidence: Section 4.3, PDF p.9; Figure 4, PDF p.8; cited SDAG reference, PDF p.14
C_rationale: The survey accurately describes the architectural difference and security property of SDAG (Dekel et al., 2026). SDAG uses sparse attention to isolate retrieved documents from each other within the transformer generator, making it more difficult for a single malicious document to contaminate the context or influence the interpretation of other retrieved evidence compared to standard causal attention.
C_evidence: Section 4.3, PDF p.9; Figure 4, PDF p.8

source_title: Comprehensive Comparison of RAG Methods Across Multi-Domain Conversational QA
exact_quote: This disconnect is most pronounced for DoQA, where MRR exceeds 90% but F1 remains below 40%, highlighting that strong retrieval does not necessarily translate into strong generation
A_rationale: In Table 2, DoQA MRR@5 values exceed 90 for several methods (Vanilla 92.0, Reranker 93.1, HyDE 90.9) while all DoQA F1 scores remain below 40 (max 36.9). Table 3 confirms a negative Spearman correlation (-0.157) for DoQA, supporting the observed disconnect. The claim's numbers and direction match the evidence within the same harness.
A_evidence: Table 2 (DoQA column, PDF p.6); Section 5.6 and Table 3 ρ=-0.157 (PDF p.7)
B_rationale: Table 2 shows DoQA F1 below 40 for every evaluated RAG method. However, only Vanilla RAG, Reranker, Query Rewriting, and HyDE exceed 90 MRR@5; the other four methods range from 84.5 to 85.3, so the unqualified dataset-level wording overstates the result. The paired high-MRR and low-F1 cases still support the narrower conclusion that strong retrieval does not necessarily yield strong answer F1.
B_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.6 (printed p.238); Figure 3 and Section 5.6, PDF p.7 (printed p.239); experimental setup and metrics in Sections 5.1-5.3, PDF pp.5-6
C_rationale: Table 2 shows that for the DoQA dataset, the retriever performance (MRR@5) exceeds 80% and indeed exceeds 90% for several methods (Vanilla RAG, Reranker, Query Rewriting, HyDE), whereas the generator performance (F1) remains consistently below 40% (ranging from 21.6% to 38.2% across all rows including Oracle). This confirms the pronounced disconnect between retrieval and generation performance on this dataset.
C_evidence: Table 2 and Figure 3, PDF p. 6-7

source_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
source_section: Appendix B.1 Fine-Tuning Full Results and Discussion
exact_quote: We verify that the FT variants have a higher rate of generating correct answers (%C) compared to closed-book and Vanilla RAG for Musique but not for HotPotQA
A_rationale: The claim says FT variants have higher %C than closed-book and Vanilla RAG for Musique, but Table 3 shows Data Mix 2 and 3 (both 23%) are lower than Vanilla RAG (28.8%) for Musique — only Data Mix 1 (31.4%) exceeds it. The 'not for HotPotQA' portion holds (all FT < 46.6). The general 'FT variants' phrasing overstates the Musique result, so a narrower claim is warranted.
A_evidence: Table 3, PDF p.17
B_rationale: For Musique, only Data Mix 1 reaches 31.4% correct and exceeds both closed-book at 6.6% and Vanilla RAG at 28.8%; Data Mixes 2 and 3 each score 23.0% and therefore do not exceed Vanilla RAG. For HotPotQA, the fine-tuned variants score 41.2% to 43.4%, which is below Vanilla RAG at 46.6% but above closed-book at 32.0%. The blanket contrast involving the FT variants and both baselines is therefore too broad, although the table supports a more specific comparison.
B_evidence: Table 3 and Fine-tuning Results and Discussion in Appendix B.1, PDF p.17; model and fine-tuning settings in Appendix A.1-A.2, PDF p.15
C_rationale: The authors claim that 'the FT variants' (plural) have a higher rate of generating correct answers (%C) compared to closed-book and Vanilla RAG for Musique. However, Table 3 shows that only Data Mix 1 (31.4%C) outperforms Vanilla RAG (28.8%C) on Musique, while Data Mix 2 and 3 both score lower (23.0%C) than Vanilla RAG. Because Data Mix 2 and 3 are direct counterexamples to the generalized statement for Musique, the claim is only partially supported and must be narrowed to specify Data Mix 1.
C_evidence: Table 3, PDF p.17

A_rationale: Over raw baselines, Table 2 xRAG entries are NQ 0.293/0.126 and TriviaQA 0.152/0.043; the TriviaQA Mixtral value (4.3%) falls below the claimed 10% lower bound, so the 10-29% range is not fully accurate. The direction against retrieval baselines (B+R: -0.085, -0.002 negative; 0.047, 0.054 marginal) is well supported. The over-retrieval conclusion holds but the raw-baseline percentage range is overstated at its lower end.
A_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.13; Section 5.1 text, PDF p.14
B_rationale: Table 2 reports raw-baseline gains of 15.2% and 29.3% for Mistral-7B, but 4.3% and 12.6% for Mixtral-8x7B. The 4.3% TriviaQA result directly contradicts the claimed lower bound of 10%. The retrieval-baseline entries are -0.2%, -8.5%, +5.4%, and +4.7%, supporting the narrower characterization of those gains as negative or marginal.
B_evidence: Table 2 and its caption, PDF p.13; Section 5.1, PDF p.14
C_rationale: Table 2 shows xRAG (Mistral-7B) achieves 15.2% and 29.3% gains over B (raw LLM) on TriviaQA and NQ, while its gains over B+R (retrieval baseline) are -0.2% and -8.5% (negative). For xRAG (Mixtral-8x7B), gains over B are 4.3% and 12.6%, while gains over B+R are 5.4% and 4.7% (marginal). This completely matches the claim's description.
C_evidence: Table 2, PDF p. 13; Section 5.1, PDF p. 14

source_section: 5.1 Comparative Analysis of Framework Performance on Short-Form QA
exact_quote: FiD-Light, although also a generator-side enhancement, adopts a different optimization philosophy centered on lightweight, efficient fusion of retrieved documents during decoding, yielding more moderate improvements of 18-27% across TriviaQA and NQ
A_rationale: Table 2 shows FiD-Light with TriviaQA EM improvement 0.185 (18.5%) and NQ EM improvement 0.27 (27%) over the raw baseline, matching the claimed 18-27% range. SELF-RAG's larger PopQA/ARC gains provide the contrast to FiD-Light's more moderate improvements. Numbers and direction are consistent with the table.
A_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.13; Section 5.1 text, PDF p.14
B_rationale: Table 2 supports the stated FiD-Light values of 0.185 and 0.27, corresponding to 18.5% and 27% over its raw baseline. The broader contrast with SELF-RAG is not consistently directional: SELF-RAG has much larger reported TriviaQA gains but a -50.5% NQ entry, while the methods also use different backbones and EM versus accuracy. The surveyed ablation discussion does not isolate lightweight fusion as the cause of the reported gains.
B_evidence: Table 1, PDF p.12; Table 2 and Section 5 introduction, PDF p.13; Section 5.1, PDF p.14; Section 5.4, PDF p.17
C_rationale: The claim correctly quotes FiD-Light's improvements (18% and 27% in Table 2 are shown as 0.185 and 0.27). However, evaluating this as a 'more moderate' improvement compared to SELF-RAG is a cross-source synthesis where the baselines, backbones (FiD+DPR vs LLaMA-2), and metric implementations (EM vs Acc) are completely uncontrolled. Thus, a narrower claim focusing purely on FiD-Light's individual performance is supported.
C_evidence: Table 2, PDF p. 13; Section 5.1, PDF p. 14

source_title: Trustworthiness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems: A Survey
exact_quote: Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) [1] shows that adversaries can embed malicious instructions within retrieved documents, effectively controlling the model’s behavior without modifying the input prompt.
A_rationale: The survey accurately reports IPI's mechanism: malicious instructions embedded in retrieved documents control model behavior without altering the user's input prompt. Table 3 lists IPI as Interaction-level, Generator object, key mechanism 'Indirect prompt injection', black-box, consistent with the prose. The contrast between document-carried control and input-prompt modification is faithfully represented as the distinguishing feature. This is a descriptive restatement of a single cited work, supported by the paper's own taxonomy.
A_evidence: PDF p.13 (Interaction-level Attacks section); Table 3, PDF p.14 (IPI row); Table 2, PDF p.12
B_rationale: The interaction-level discussion on PDF p.13 explicitly states that IPI places malicious instructions in retrieved documents while leaving the input prompt unmodified. Table 3 independently classifies IPI as a black-box, generator-targeting indirect prompt-injection attack, and Table 2 also identifies it as a generator-directed attack. The claim asserts that direct prompt modification is unnecessary rather than claiming that indirect injection outperforms direct injection, and the checked material contains no counterexample to that scoped capability claim.
B_evidence: Interaction-level Attacks, PDF p.13; Table 3, PDF p.14; Table 2, PDF p.12
C_rationale: The claim accurately describes the mechanism of Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) based on the cited reference. IPI works by embedding malicious instructions in the retrieved context rather than the direct user prompt, allowing attackers to hijack model behavior without modifying the input. The literature cited firmly establishes this distinct attack vector and its effectiveness compared to direct prompt modification.
C_evidence: Section 3.2.3, PDF p. 13

source_title: Sufficient Context: A New Lens on Retrieval Augmented Generation Systems
source_section: 5.1 Selective RAG Using Sufficient Context Signal (Results)
exact_quote: see gains of over 10% for Gemma 27B on HotpotQA in the highest accuracy regions, and gains of over 5% for Gemini 1.5 Pro on the same dataset near the 70% coverage region
A_rationale: The claim describes magnitude of gains for combining the sufficient-context signal with confidence versus confidence alone, for Gemma 27B and Gemini 1.5 Pro on HotpotQA. Figure 4's HotpotQA panels show the purple (combined) curves above the gray (confidence-only) curves in the described regions, consistent with the stated >10% and >5% gains. Exact numeric verification from the plotted curves is approximate, but the direction and rough magnitude are supported.
A_evidence: Section 5.1 Results, PDF p.9; Figure 4, PDF p.10
B_rationale: Figure 4 shows the Gemma 27B combined-signal curve more than 10 percentage points above its confidence-only baseline in the low-coverage, high-accuracy region. The Gemini 1.5 Pro panel shows a gap exceeding five points near 70% coverage. The quote explicitly identifies the different operating regions, so it reports two qualified within-model gains rather than asserting an uncontrolled direct ranking between the models.
B_evidence: Section 5.1 Results, PDF p.9; Figure 4 top-left and top-right panels and caption, PDF p.10
C_rationale: Figure 4 clearly illustrates the accuracy-coverage trade-off curves for both models on HotpotQA. Near the 70% coverage region, Gemini 1.5 Pro shows a gain of over 5% (moving from ~70% to ~76% accuracy). For Gemma 27B in the highest accuracy regions (low coverage, around 10%), the gain is over 10% (moving from ~82% to ~93% accuracy).
C_evidence: Figure 4, PDF page 10

source_title: Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
source_section: 5 Other Considerations for Abstention (Following up After Abstention)
exact_quote: Abstention should not be viewed as the termination of a conversation, but rather as a step towards subsequent information acquisition
A_rationale: This is a purely normative recommendation contrasting an abstention-as-termination framing against an abstention-as-inquiry-trigger framing. The survey provides no shared utility, cost, or outcome measurement comparing the two framings; it merely cites illustrative works. Per the manual's policy rule, an action/framing recommendation without a common utility basis does not constitute a supported comparative claim.
A_evidence: PDF p.13 (printed p.541), Section 5 'Following up After Abstention'
B_rationale: The section states this recommendation and identifies asking the user or retrieving data as possible follow-up actions, but it reports no experiment comparing conversation termination with information acquisition. Table 1 and the surveyed metrics evaluate static answering and abstention outcomes rather than downstream dialogue utility, follow-up costs, or safety stakes. The categorical policy preference therefore lacks the common utility specification needed to support the word “should.”
B_evidence: Section 5, 'Following up After Abstention,' PDF p.13 (printed p.541); Section 4.2, Table 1 and abstention metrics, PDF pp.10–11 (printed pp.538–539).
C_rationale: The claim proposes a shift in perspective from viewing abstention as a conversational endpoint to treating it as an interactive transition. The authors support this normative claim by synthesizing existing literature (e.g., Feng et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2024b) that demonstrates how systems can dynamically ask for clarification or retrieve new data post-abstention. As a survey-level conceptual claim, it is logically consistent with the cited frameworks and the paper's overarching taxonomy.
C_evidence: Section 5, Following up After Abstention, PDF p. 13 (printed p. 541)

source_title: Do not Abstain! Identify and Solve the Uncertainty
exact_quote: judging by the inquiry and the answer can help to increase the performance, directly judging based on the inquiry can help the model to better judge the source of uncertainty
A_rationale: Table 5 reports uncertainty classification accuracy for prompt, inquiry, and answer variants across six models on the same benchmarks. In every row inquiry beats prompt (e.g., GPT-4o avg 0.4938 vs 0.5692) and answer is highest (0.6062), confirming that judging via inquiry improves over direct prompting and that inquiry-answer adds further gains. The comparison is a controlled self-baseline within one harness. Direction and strength match the wording.
A_evidence: Table 5, PDF p.8; Section 6, PDF p.8
B_rationale: In Table 5, both the inquiry and answer variants have higher average uncertainty-classification accuracy than direct prompt judging for each of the six evaluated models. Several individual model-dataset cells are counterexamples, including the Qwen2.5-72B inquiry result on HotpotQA and the Mistral-7B inquiry result on ToolBench. Because the wording says the methods can help rather than claiming uniform improvement, the consistent model-level average gains support its stated direction, although uncertainty intervals are not reported.
B_evidence: Metric definitions, PDF p.4 (printed p.17180); Sections 5.1-5.2, PDF pp.6-7; Table 5 and Section 6, PDF p.8; continuation of experimental details, PDF p.9.
C_rationale: Table 5 shows the classification performance of directly prompting (prompt), judging after generating an inquiry (inquiry), and judging based on the inquiry answer (answer). For all six evaluated models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B), the performance ranks consistently as: answer > inquiry > prompt, validating both parts of the claim.
C_evidence: Section 6, PDF p.8; Table 5, PDF p.8

source_title: Securing Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Taxonomy of Attacks, Defenses, and Future Directions
exact_quote: In our setting, the attacker controls or influences part of the external knowledge a RAG system reaches, such as content to be ingested, retrievable pages or files, agent memory, or the queries sent to the interface, but not the model’s parameters or the user’s prompt.
A_rationale: This is a definitional threat-model statement contrasting attacker control over external-knowledge surfaces (ingestion, retrievable pages, memory, interface queries) with no control over model parameters or user prompt. The paper consistently articulates this boundary in the Introduction, Figure 1/2, and Section 2.2. It is a self-consistent scoping distinction rather than an empirical result, and the two capability sides are clearly and correctly delineated. The claim faithfully reflects the survey's stated operational boundary.
A_evidence: Section 2.2 Threat Model, PDF p.3; Figure 2 p.3; Introduction p.1
B_rationale: Section 2.2 explicitly grants the attacker influence over external knowledge and interface-query surfaces while excluding control of model parameters and the user's prompt. Figure 2 and Section 2.3 consistently enforce this operational boundary, so the quote accurately states the paper's scoped threat-model definition rather than an empirical result requiring experimental controls.
B_evidence: Section 2.2, PDF p.3; Figure 2, PDF p.3; Section 2.3, PDF p.4
C_rationale: The quote accurately describes the operational threat model defined by the authors. They explicitly state that the attacker controls or influences external knowledge surfaces but does not control the model parameters or the user prompt. This boundary is consistently applied throughout the taxonomy.
C_evidence: Section 2.2, PDF p.3

source_title: Comprehensive Comparison of RAG Methods Across Multi-Domain Conversational QA
exact_quote: This is evident in the F1 range difference between Doc2Dial (Feng et al., 2020), centered on specialized, open-ended questions in comparison to the factoid-style questions of CoQA (Reddy et al., 2019)
A_rationale: The observable F1 range difference between Doc2Dial (low ~20s) and CoQA (high 47-74) is factually present in Table 2. However the causal attribution to the 'model's internal knowledge' of dataset topics/formats is not isolated by any controlled manipulation or ablation. Only the descriptive F1 difference is supported, so the causal framing must be narrowed.
A_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.6; Section 5.6-5.8 PDF p.7-9
B_rationale: Table 2 supports a substantial descriptive difference between the F1 ranges for Doc2Dial and CoQA. However, the datasets also differ in domain, answer length and structure, corpus characteristics, prompts, and other properties, and the paper does not manipulate question style or directly measure internal knowledge. The observed cross-dataset association therefore cannot establish the implied explanation involving format or model knowledge.
B_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.6 (printed p.238); dataset and answer-format discussion, PDF p.7 (printed p.239); Sections 5.7-5.8, PDF pp.8-9 (printed pp.240-241)
C_rationale: The claim describes a substantial difference in generator F1 score ranges between the Doc2Dial and CoQA datasets. Table 2 provides the empirical support: Doc2Dial F1 scores across all configurations are in the lower range of 21.1 to 37.0, while CoQA F1 scores are in the much higher range of 28.9 to 83.9, verifying the distinct range difference described.
C_evidence: Table 2, PDF p. 6

source_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
exact_quote: Notably, in generative tasks, ASR requires nuance due to variations in language expression. For example, responses like “Sam Altman” and “The CEO of OpenAI is Sam Altman” both correctly answer “Who is the CEO of OpenAI?” Thus, researchers often employ substring matching rather than exact matching for this evaluation
A_rationale: The claim is a descriptive methodological observation contrasting exact matching with substring matching for ASR scoring in generative attack evaluation. The survey justifies this with a clear example (multiple phrasings correctly answering the same question) and cites PoisonedRAG [232], which does employ substring matching. The comparison of the two scoring approaches and the stated preference for substring matching are consistent with the cited evaluation practice, and no counterexample or numeric mismatch is at issue. The claim uses hedged language ('often'), and the direction/scope are faithfully represented.
A_evidence: Section 5.3 Safety Evaluation – Metrics, PDF p.17
B_rationale: The example on PDF p.17 correctly shows that full-response exact matching would distinguish two substantively equivalent answers, while target-answer substring matching can accept both. The section cites PoisonedRAG [232] for this evaluation practice, supporting the narrower method-specific statement. However, it provides neither a systematic metric audit nor multiple documented examples establishing the broader prevalence qualifier that researchers "often" use substring matching rather than exact matching.
B_evidence: Section 5.3, Metrics, PDF p.17; surrounding safety taxonomy and threat-model discussion, PDF pp.15-17; Section 5.4, Evaluation, PDF p.18
C_rationale: The claim accurately describes a common evaluation practice in generative safety literature. In generative tasks, strict exact matching would fail to recognize correct answers when they are embedded in longer sentences. Thus, as seen in PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., 2024), substring matching is typically used to calculate the Attack Success Rate (ASR) to handle natural variations in language expression.
C_evidence: Section 5.3 Safety Evaluation - Metrics, PDF p.17; and reference [232] (Zou et al., 2024)

source_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Survey of Architectures, Enhancements, and Robustness Frontiers
source_section: 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Framework Performance on Multi-Hop QA

A_rationale: Table 2 shows FLAREdirect GPT-3.5 on 2Wiki as 0.622/0.223 (F1), matching the claimed 62% improvement over the raw LLM and 22% over standard retrieval. Both quantities and directions are faithful to the table. The single-cell numeric claim has no counterexample.
A_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.13 (FLAREdirect GPT-3.5 2Wiki 0.622/0.223 F1); Section 5.2, PDF p.15
B_rationale: Table 2 reports FLAREdirect on 2Wiki as 0.622/0.223 F1 relative to the raw backbone and retrieval-augmented baselines. The paper explicitly explains that these decimal values denote relative gains, making them 62.2% and 22.3%, which support the rounded percentages in the claim. The table caption identifies B and B+R as the same backbone without and with standard retrieval, although detailed retrieval and prompting controls are not reproduced.
B_evidence: Table 2, PDF p.13; Section 5 introduction, PDF p.13; Section 5.1 metric interpretation, PDF p.14; Section 5.2, PDF p.15
C_rationale: In Table 2, under Hybrid RAG, FLAREdirect with GPT-3.5 backbone on the 2Wiki dataset has a reported relative gain of 0.622 (62.2%) over the raw backbone (B) and 0.223 (22.3%) over standard retrieval (B+R). These figures directly support the claim of 62% and 22% improvements respectively.
C_evidence: Table 2 on PDF page 13; Section 5.2 on PDF page 15

source_title: Comprehensive Comparison of RAG Methods Across Multi-Domain Conversational QA
exact_quote: most datasets have a relatively high correlation between the F1 and MRR values
A_rationale: Table 3 shows six of eight datasets with ρ ≥ 0.62 (QuAC 0.620, QReCC 0.857, TopiOCQA 0.874, Doc2Dial 0.687, CoQA 0.762, INSCIT 0.788), so 'most datasets have a relatively high correlation' is supported. The stated exceptions SQA (0.383) and DoQA (-0.157) match the low/negative values. The description is faithful.
A_evidence: Table 3, PDF p.7 (Spearman's rho per dataset); Section 5.6
B_rationale: Table 3 reports correlations of 0.620, 0.857, 0.874, 0.687, 0.762, and 0.788 for six of the eight datasets. Only SQA is weakly positive at 0.383 and DoQA is negative at -0.157, exactly matching the stated exceptions. Thus a majority of datasets exhibit moderate-to-high positive F1–MRR correlation.
B_evidence: Table 3 and Section 5.6, PDF p.7 (printed p.239); Table 2 and Sections 5.1-5.3, PDF pp.5-6 (printed pp.237-238)
C_rationale: Table 3 lists the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rho) for each dataset. Six out of the eight datasets (QuAC, QReCC, TopiOCQA, Doc2Dial, CoQA, and INSCIT) exhibit moderate to strong positive correlations (ranging from 0.620 to 0.874), while only SQA (0.383) and DoQA (-0.157) are exceptions. Thus, the claim that most datasets have a relatively high correlation is fully supported.
C_evidence: Table 3, PDF p. 7

source_title: Do not Abstain! Identify and Solve the Uncertainty
exact_quote: if the model fails to generate an inquiry of high quality, the advantages of a more concise input may be overshadowed by the drawbacks of a poor inquiry, resulting in suboptimal performance, and a good inquiry can help the model to gather more useful information
A_rationale: The claim asserts a causal chain: poor inquiry causes suboptimal performance and good inquiry gathers useful information. Figure 4 only shows a correlational relationship between inquiry score and the percentage of errors caused by bad inquiry; there is no controlled manipulation isolating inquiry quality while holding other factors fixed. Per the manual, a causal claim backed only by correlation is at most partial. The descriptive, correlational version is supported.
A_evidence: Figure 4, PDF p.6; Section 5.2, PDF p.7
B_rationale: Figure 4 reports low inquiry quality among a subset of correctly classified cases with incorrect answers, which supports an association between poor inquiries and some failures. The paper does not independently manipulate inquiry quality while holding the model, retrieved information, interaction route, and other factors fixed. InteractDPO also changes the training and feedback procedure, so its gains in Table 6 do not isolate inquiry quality as the causal mechanism.
B_evidence: Figure 4 and its caption, PDF p.6 (printed p.17182); Section 5.2, PDF p.7; Table 6 and experiment description, PDF pp.8-9.
C_rationale: The paper evaluates the downstream impact of inquiry quality on final model performance. Figure 4 shows that a significant fraction of errors across multiple models is caused specifically by poor-quality inquiries, while Table 6 shows that optimizing inquiry quality via InteractDPO leads to superior overall performance.
C_evidence: Section 5.2, PDF p.7; Figure 4, PDF p.6

source_title: Towards Trustworthy Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
source_section: 4.2 Data Leakage From the External Retrieval Database
exact_quote: Although distinct from direct extraction methods and based on a different threat model, membership inference attacks have also proven effective for data extraction.
A_rationale: The survey asserts MIA is 'effective for data extraction' but the text itself notes MIA infers whether content is present rather than directly extracting it, and section 4.1.2 calls it 'not a direct privacy attack.' Thus equating MIA effectiveness with extraction effectiveness overstates; the two approaches lack a common quantitative estimand and no comparative numbers are given. A narrower descriptive claim about MIA revealing sensitive information is supported.
A_evidence: Section 4.2, PDF p.13; Table 3, PDF p.12
B_rationale: The survey's own task taxonomy distinguishes document extraction from membership inference: the former extracts confidential content, whereas the latter determines whether specified passages are present. Table 3 likewise assigns Liu et al. to membership inference rather than document extraction, and Section 4.1.2 calls membership inference not a direct privacy attack. Because the methods have different threat models, outputs, and evaluation units, the paper does not support treating membership inference as having proven effective for the same data-extraction outcome as direct extraction.
B_evidence: PDF p.12, Table 3; PDF p.13, Sections 4.1.2 and 4.2; PDF p.14, Section 4.5
C_rationale: The claim asserts that membership inference attacks are effective for 'data extraction.' This is a conceptual error because membership inference attacks only determine whether a known document is present in the database, whereas direct extraction attacks retrieve unknown documents. Comparing them as both being effective for 'data extraction' is logically invalid.
C_evidence: Section 4.2, PDF p. 13

source_title: Do not Abstain! Identify and Solve the Uncertainty
exact_quote: the responses in the dataset are usually generated by different LLMs (Rafailov et al., 2024; Qi et al., 2024). Thus, the feedback is usually purely offline
A_rationale: This is a descriptive/definitional characterization contrasting vanilla DPO's offline preference data (responses generated by other LLMs collected ahead of training) with the paper's proposed on-policy scheme. The statement accurately reflects standard DPO practice and is supported by the cited works (Rafailov et al., Qi et al.). It is a background contrast, not an empirical claim requiring the paper's own tables. The characterization is faithful and uncontested.
A_evidence: Section 5.2, PDF p.7 (printed 17183)
B_rationale: Section 5.2 explicitly contrasts pre-collected DPO preferences with InteractDPO's generation of inquiries during training, so the offline-versus-on-policy distinction is supported. The broader assertion that responses in vanilla DPO datasets are usually generated by different LLMs is not established by an audit or empirical summary; only two citations are supplied, one of which is itself an online-DPO method. C_rationale: Figure 3 illustrates that each prompt-based baseline occupies a single, static point on the risk-coverage plane.
